verses.text: Woe to those who decree unrighteous decrees, and to the writers who write oppressive decrees;
to deprive the needy from justice, and to rob the poor among my people of their rights, that widows may be their plunder, and that they may make the fatherless their prey!
What will you do in the day of visitation, and in the desolation which will come from afar? To whom will you flee for help? Where will you leave your wealth?
They will only bow down under the prisoners, and will fall under the slain. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.
Alas Assyrian, the rod of my anger, the staff in whose hand is my indignation!
I will send him against a profane nation, and against the people who anger me will I give him a command to take the plunder and to take the prey, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets.
However he doesn’t mean so, neither does his heart think so; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off not a few nations.
For he says, “Aren’t all of my princes kings?
Isn’t Calno like Carchemish? Isn’t Hamath like Arpad? Isn’t Samaria like Damascus?”
As my hand has found the kingdoms of the idols, whose engraved images exceeded those of Jerusalem and of Samaria;
shall I not, as I have done to Samaria and her idols, so do to Jerusalem and her idols?

Therefore it will happen that, when the Lord has performed his whole work on Mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the willful proud heart of the king of Assyria, and the insolence of his haughty looks.

For he has said, “By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom; for I have understanding: and I have removed the boundaries of the peoples, and have robbed their treasures. Like a valiant man I have brought down their rulers.

My hand has found the riches of the peoples like a nest, and like one gathers eggs that are abandoned, I have gathered all the earth. There was no one who moved their wing, or that opened their mouth, or chirped.”

Should an ax brag against him who chops with it? Should a saw exalt itself above him who saws with it? As if a rod should lift those who lift it up, or as if a staff should lift up someone who is not wood.
Therefore the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will send among his fat ones leanness; and under his glory a burning will be kindled like the burning of fire.
The light of Israel will be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame; and it will burn and devour his thorns and his briers in one day.
He will consume the glory of his forest, and of his fruitful field, both soul and body. It will be as when a standard bearer faints.
The remnant of the trees of his forest shall be few, so that a child could write their number.

It will come to pass in that day that the remnant of Israel, and those who have escaped from the house of Jacob will no more again lean on him who struck them, but shall lean on Yahweh, the Holy One of Israel, in truth.
A remnant will return, even the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God.
For though your people, Israel, are like the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. A destruction is determined, overflowing with righteousness.
For the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will make a full end, and that determined, throughout all the earth.
Therefore the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, says “My people who dwell in Zion, don’t be afraid of the Assyrian, though he strike you with the rod, and lift up his staff against you, as Egypt did.
For yet a very little while, and the indignation against you will be accomplished, and my anger will be directed to his destruction.”
Yahweh of Armies will stir up a scourge against him, as in the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb. His rod will be over the sea, and he will lift it up like he did against Egypt.
It will happen in that day, that his burden will depart from off your shoulder, and his yoke from off your neck, and the yoke shall be destroyed because of the anointing oil.
He has come to Aiath. He has passed through Migron. At Michmash he stores his baggage.
They have gone over the pass. They have taken up their lodging at Geba. Ramah trembles. Gibeah of Saul has fled.
Cry aloud with your voice, daughter of Gallim! Listen, Laishah! You poor Anathoth!
Madmenah is a fugitive. The inhabitants of Gebim flee for safety.
This very day he will halt at Nob. He shakes his hand at the mountain of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem.
Behold, the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will lop the boughs with terror. The tall will be cut down, and the lofty will be brought low.
He will cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon will fall by the Mighty One.

footnotes.content: Isaiah opens with a groan against those who twist the law to crush the helpless. The grieving God sees every unjust decree, every law written to rob rather than serve. When power becomes a tool to harm, the Lord himself stands as judge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The specificity cuts deep—widows and the fatherless, the poorest among us, targeted as prey. This is not abstract injustice; it's hunting the defenseless. Jesus would later insist: the least ones matter most to the Father.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A day is coming when the powerful will have nowhere to hide, no riches to save them. Isaiah asks the oppressor a haunting question: Where will you run when God's judgment arrives? There is no escape from His hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The oppressors bow under prisoners and fall under the dead—their dominion turned to rubble. Yet even after judgment falls, God's anger is not yet finished; His hand remains extended. Grace delays, but justice will come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A shocking move: God calls Assyria His rod, His tool of correction. Even the great empires are instruments in God's hand, whether they know it or not. Power without recognition of whose hand holds it is blind.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God sends the Assyrian against those who anger Him, yet He frames it as a command—to plunder, to tread down. Judgment flows through human hands; the Lord uses earthly powers as instruments of His will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is the crucial turn: Assyria does not know it serves God. The king thinks only of conquest and destruction, not of bearing God's judgment. When hearts are bent on pride, they cannot see the hand that moves them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Assyrian boasts of his princes as kings. Arrogance speaks loudest just before the fall. Every king who confuses his own strength with his own wisdom is on the verge of learning otherwise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Samaria, Damascus—a catalog of conquered cities, each a trophy of Assyrian might. The king lines them up as proof of invincibility, not seeing that their very downfall foreshadows his own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Assyrian takes credit for finding the kingdoms of idols, as if human cleverness seized what his gods had blessed. But all idols, no matter how grand their carved images, are powerless before the living God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What Assyria did to Samaria and her idols, he assumes he will do to Jerusalem. But Jerusalem is not merely another conquest on the list—it is God's own city, and His protection over it is not the same as His judgment through Assyrian hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A turning point: When the Lord has accomplished His full work—using Assyria as His rod—He will then turn and punish Assyria itself for her pride and arrogance. Tools can be set down once their work is done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king of Assyria claims all victories for himself: 'By my hand, by my wisdom.' No mention of providence, no acknowledgment of the Lord. This is the pride that precedes the fall—when strength and cleverness blind us to grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Like a man gathering abandoned eggs from a nest, Assyria has plundered treasures with no resistance. Unchecked power grows drunker on its own success, never noticing the moment when the Lord will reach out and take the cup from its hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Should an ax boast against the one who wields it? A piercing image—the tool that claims its own power forgets who swings it. Assyria, thinking itself the wielder, is in truth only the instrument in God's hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord sends leanness among Assyria's fat ones; under her glory a burning will kindle like fire. Pride becomes fuel for its own consumption. What seemed invincible will wither from within.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel's light becomes a fire, the Lord's Holy One becomes a flame that consumes thorns and briers. Those who prick and harm God's people will be burned away in a single day—God's judgment is both swift and thorough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Glory and fruitful fields, soul and body—all that Assyria prizes will be consumed. The glory that stood so proudly will wither like a standard bearer collapsing mid-battle. Earthly splendor is fragile before God's judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What remains of the forest will be so few that a child could count the trees. Utter devastation is measured in the powerlessness of what's left—a stark picture of how thoroughly the Lord strips away what seemed permanent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In that day, Israel will cease leaning on the one who struck them and will lean instead on Yahweh in truth. Judgment brings conversion; when Assyria's power is broken, Israel sees clearly that only the Lord's hand can sustain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A remnant will return to the mighty God. Not all Israel, but a faithful few—those who survive and recognize that survival itself is a gift from God's hand, not their own strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Though Israel were as numerous as the sand, only a remnant returns. A destruction is determined, yet it flows with righteousness—God's judgment is not arbitrary but rooted in what is right and true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord will make a full end throughout all the earth—judgment is complete, not partial, not negotiated away. Yet even in finality, God's character remains righteous; nothing is done without purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To those in Zion trembling before the Assyrian, the Lord says: 'Don't be afraid.' Even as Assyria strikes with rod and staff as Egypt once did, God's people are not abandoned. Fear yields to trust when we remember whose hand truly holds all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Yet a very little while'—God promises an end to indignation. The Assyrian's anger will burn itself out; the Lord's anger will turn upon him instead. Time works with God, not against His faithful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord will stir up a scourge as in the slaughter at Midian and Oreb—echoes of old victories where God moved against overwhelming odds. His rod will be over the sea as He lifted it against Egypt. The Lord who freed His people once will do so again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The burden will depart from your shoulder; the yoke will be destroyed because of the anointing oil. Deliverance comes to the Lord's anointed people through His power, not through human strength. What oppresses us yields only to His hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aiath, Migron, Michmash—the invader's march detailed with precision, each place a landmark on the road toward Jerusalem. The catalog of places is real geography, urgent and immediate; the threat is not distant but drawing near.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They pass the summit, lodge at Geba. Ramah trembles; Gibeah of Saul has fled. The advance is relentless, place by place; the inhabitants scatter in terror. It is the picture of invasion, fear spreading like a wave.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cry aloud, Gallim; listen, Laishah; poor Anathoth. The cry is personal—specific towns and their inhabitants called to witness the march of the invader. Each place has a voice, each person is seen by the prophet and by God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Madmenah flees; Gebim's inhabitants flee for safety. All that remains is panic, flight, the dissolution of ordered life as the army advances. Yet even in this devastation, the prophet is watching; the Lord sees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This very day he will halt at Nob, shakes his hand at the mountain of the daughter of Zion—Jerusalem itself. The invader stands at the gates, arrogant, threatening God's own city. But halting is not conquering; proximity is not victory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Behold, the Lord will lop the boughs with terror; the tall will be cut down, the lofty brought low. The Lord Himself now acts as pruner, cutting away what towers in pride. What seemed insurmountable yields to His hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He will cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon will fall by the Mighty One. Readers today hear an echo in these words—how pride in human power, like dense forest or majestic Lebanon, falls before the one true Strength. Empires rise, but their boasting is heard by the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
